## Finding the lost plants

Every plant in this list is a search waiting to happen. This tool suggests where to begin from the pattern of past
sightings alone, applying one component of our
[protocol for detecting local extinction](https://imerss.github.io/detecting-local-extinction/docs/assessing_extirpation_risk/).

**Extirpation probability (EP)** runs from 0 (likely still present) to 1 (likely lost locally). Using
[Solow's (1993)](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2307/1940821) method, it compares when a species was
sighted with the whole period of record, from the earliest collection in our data (1859) to 2025. EP is highest for
plants that were recorded repeatedly and then stopped being seen. Plants recorded only once or twice tend to score
nearer the middle, since so few records say little either way.

**Five steps to a target species:**

1. **Choose a plant.** The table lists the highest EP first. Tick a species, and use *Filters* to narrow the list, for
   example to native species.
2. **See where it grew.** Each circle on the map is a group of sightings treated as one population, coloured by its EP.
   Hover over one for its *Cluster EP*. A smaller *Population radius* can reveal sites where a plant has gone unseen
   even though it persists elsewhere. A ⚠ marks plants with records that have no coordinates and so cannot be mapped.
3. **Read its history.** Open *Records* to see who found it, when and where. The dates show what time of year it was
   collected.
4. **Go looking.** Search the places and habitats where it was last recorded, at the season it was last seen.
5. **Share what you find.** Post your photos to iNaturalist through the
   ["Lost" Plants of the Saanich Peninsula](https://www.inaturalist.org/projects/lost-plants-of-the-saanich-peninsula)
   project. Whatever you find, the search itself adds to what we know.

**A high EP is a reason to go looking, not proof of loss.** It does not account for where or how hard people have
searched, or for suitable habitat, which the full protocol goes on to weigh.
